title: Cloudflare 2019: what users experienced
rows: Cloudflare sits between visitors and websites. Its servers deliver content and screen requests before they reach a website’s own server.
On July 2, a firewall rule update overloaded servers worldwide. Visitors saw “502 Bad Gateway” errors instead of web pages.
The outage lasted 27 minutes. CPU usage reached 100%, and Cloudflare’s traffic fell 82% at its worst.
Why it mattered: one shared provider’s failure interrupted many customers at once, even when their own websites were otherwise healthy.
note:
Explain the setup as an intermediary: a visitor’s request passes through Cloudflare before reaching the site. A 502 error means that intermediary could not obtain the response it needed. The 82% figure describes Cloudflare’s traffic drop, not 82% of the Internet.
An everyday example: a visitor may be unable to open a store or complete an online task. This is an illustration of availability impact, not a measured financial-loss claim.
Sources: https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-outage/
https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/

title: The technical trigger: expensive pattern matching
rows: The web application firewall (WAF) checks requests for suspicious content. This update targeted malicious JavaScript.
A regular expression, or regex, is a text-search pattern. The simplified fragment .*.*=.* contains overlapping “match anything” sections.
Backtracking means retrying different ways to match the same text. Here, the repeated work consumed the CPU needed to serve requests.
“Simulate” mode only stopped the rule from blocking visitors. It still ran the expensive check on real traffic.
note:
Read the pattern aloud as: any text, followed by any text, followed by an equals sign, then any text. This is a simplified fragment, not the complete deployed expression.
Illustrative example: when a candidate input lacks an equals sign, a backtracking matcher can repeatedly redistribute characters between the wildcard sections before deciding there is no match. A check can be logically correct yet too expensive to run on every request. Avoid calling this an infinite loop: the problem is excessive repeated work.
Sources: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/
https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-outage/
source: Sources: Cloudflare incident update and technical postmortem, July 2019

title: Why the safeguards did not catch it
rows: Earlier refactoring accidentally removed a CPU safeguard. The effort to improve performance weakened a protection against costly rules.
Tests checked which requests to allow or block. They did not catch runaway CPU use, so passing tests gave incomplete reassurance.
The rollout sent the rule worldwide without a limited trial. A local defect therefore became a global availability problem.
Recovery also depended on affected systems. Engineers struggled to access internal tools, making an emergency change harder.
note:
Case analysis: several defenses failed together. A useful test plan asks both “Does this rule classify traffic correctly?” and “Can we afford to execute it under load?”
A staged rollout exposes a small traffic sample first. Teams watch errors and CPU before expanding it. That limits how many customers encounter an undetected defect.
The debt connection is the accumulated risk in testing, deployment, and recovery procedures. The new regex triggered the incident, while existing weaknesses increased its severity.
Source: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/

title: How engineers restored service
rows: 13:42 UTC: the rule goes live. By 14:00, engineers identify the WAF as the source of CPU exhaustion.
14:07 UTC: they disable the WAF globally. By 14:09, CPU usage and traffic return to normal.
They roll back the faulty rule and test the fix. At 14:52 UTC, they restore the WAF worldwide.
The tradeoff: websites recover before WAF inspection returns. Other security protections remain active during that interval.
note:
All times refer to July 2, 2019, in UTC. A rollback restores an earlier configuration or version. Disabling the affected component first removes the immediate load, giving the team room to investigate.
Make the two recovery milestones explicit: people could access websites again at 14:09, but the WAF returned at 14:52. Traffic recovery therefore does not mean every protection was already back. The detailed postmortem gives the 14:07 termination time and 14:00 diagnosis.
Sources: https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-outage/
https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/

title: What Cloudflare changed after the outage
rows: Completed by July 12: restored the CPU safeguard and inspected all 3,868 managed rules for similar problems.
Planned testing: profile each rule’s performance. That means measuring its processing cost, beyond whether it gives the right answer.
Planned rollout: release rules in stages. Planned engine change: use RE2 or Rust regex with runtime guarantees.
Why the engine matters: RE2 bounds matching time linearly in input length for a fixed pattern, avoiding unbounded backtracking.
note:
The first bullet describes work reported complete. The following actions were announced in the July 12 postmortem, so this slide does not claim they had all shipped by that date.
RE2 explanation: for a fixed pattern, work scales proportionally with input length instead of exploding through repeated retries. This does not mean every expression takes the same time. RE2 also restricts syntax: features such as backreferences and look-around are unsupported. A migration therefore needs compatibility tests.
Sources: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/
https://github.com/google/re2
source: Sources: Cloudflare postmortem (July 12, 2019) and Google RE2 documentation

title: Lessons for maintenance, debt & refactoring
rows: Maintenance includes keeping changes safe. Fixing the broken rule restores service, while stronger tests help prevent another failure.
Technical debt can live in processes too. Saving time on rollout or testing can create larger debugging and outage costs later.
Refactoring should preserve behavior. Teams also need regression tests for safety limits that ordinary feature tests may miss.
Practical takeaway: test correctness and resource use, expand releases gradually, and rehearse recovery when normal tools are unavailable.
note:
These are the presentation’s conclusions from the case. Corrective maintenance addresses an existing defect. Preventive maintenance reduces the likelihood of future failures.
Refactoring changes a program’s internal structure while preserving external behavior. The case shows why a team must identify the protections that need to survive a code change. A proposed regression test could run difficult inputs and fail when a rule exceeds an agreed processing budget. This is a recommendation, not a claim about Cloudflare’s exact implementation.
Discussion question: If a change returns the same answers but makes the service unavailable under load, has it preserved the behavior users need?
Concept source: https://refactoring.com/
Case evidence: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/
source: Case analysis, informed by Cloudflare’s postmortem and Martin Fowler on refactoring
